articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was wonderful to see so many elementary parents at this year’s Spring Fling. Thank you to Heather Frank, Bridget Schreiber, along with our Co-chairs Caroline, Jenny, & Zeena who did an amazing job with this year’s event. Thank you to our parents who attended and supported our efforts to fundraise for our elementary programs, including extra counseling services and field trips. As we close in on the end of the school year, I am reminded that this is the time of year we recognize our school community, our staff who do amazing work every day to make our students’ education possible. We begin the month on May 1st by honoring two essential groups: our school principals, whose vision and leadership shape our school culture, and our food services teams, the unsung heroes who “fuel” our students’ days...and yes, I am owning that awkward pun. We also celebrate National Teacher Appreciation Week (May 4-8), with National Teacher Appreciation Day on May 5 and California’s Day of the Teacher on May 13. Our gratitude extends as well to the specialists who do amazing work in support of student health and development: our school nurses, honored on National School Nurse Day (May 6), and our speech-language pathologists, recognized on National Speech Pathologist Day (May 18). If you have a moment this month, we encourage you to reach out to any of these dedicated professionals who have made a difference for your child. A simple note or kind word means more than you know. We close the month with Classified School Employee Week (May 17-23), a chance to thank the colleagues who keep our schools running: all of our staff who work behind the scenes with dedication and pride. To every member of our school community being recognized this month, thank you. articles.text: After 22 years with the City of Piedmont, Planning Director Kevin Jackson has decided to retire. articles.text: Editor: I remember when my family was moving from New York and they landed in Piedmont. There were a lot of great things about Piedmont but best of all were the schools. My dad’s work was located in Silicon Valley but we still decided to move here. I remember my mom telling me that Piedmont is not only a good school system but is strong across all three levels: elementary school, middle school, and high school. This has been evident to me through my years in all three Piedmont schools. The teachers are awesome, especially teacher Bracamonte who showed me the light in reading. But the problem is for these schools to thrive we need funding. Our schools have continued to be in the top percentage for testing throughout California because these dedicated teachers get top-notch materials to boost student learning. But this isn’t just for the kids. It’s also for all homeowners, because when we keep our schools strong, the quality of Piedmont as a whole goes up. The point is the school system is top notch, and keeping it that way makes the quality of Piedmont go up. So please vote Yes for Measure H to sustain our beautiful city and community. –Cyrus Emanuelson
articles.title: Keep Piedmont schools strong; vote Yes on Measure H

articles.text: Dear Editor, I appreciated last week’s article celebrating Mr. Ted Scherman — a true legend. My children were lucky to have him as both a teacher and camp counselor, and they agree without hesitation: that guy’s a legend. What struck me even more is how many legends my kids could name from their years in the district — more than a dozen educators each who were larger than life to them and who they’ll remember well into adulthood. They’ve also had many truly great teachers, and they can distinguish between the two. Great teachers teach the material well and support their students; legends went further. They pushed them to grow, forge real connections, and make learning stick in lasting ways. Their impact extended beyond the classroom — through lunch clubs, after-school programs, coaching, and simply being a visible, trusted presence in the community. My older kid, a Physics major, is taking a Chaucer class in college because he loved reading The Canterbury Tales his senior year with Dr. Marks. That’s legendary. Mr. Scherman is retiring alongside other such standouts. This represents a significant loss to our district and is likely the beginning of a larger wave of retirements. Piedmont has an unusually high concentration of great and legendary teachers. As a parent whose kids have spent a combined 14 years in this district, I am profoundly grateful to the adults who have taught them. This is also my final year in PUSD, as my youngest graduates. That perspective makes the moment feel especially urgent. I will be voting yes on Measure H because I care deeply that future classes will get to learn from great and legendary teachers, too. The conditions that once drew and kept these remarkable educators here are different, particularly for younger teachers. It’s up to all of us in this town to invest in the youngest residents. The adults who teach and have taught our kids are deeply invested in them. We need to do our part to ensure our schools will continue to attract and retain great and legendary teachers. –Sincerely, Liz Arney
articles.title: Vote yes on Measure H to attract and retain great and legendary teachers

Piedmont’s Clean Water Program is regulated by a Municipal Regional Permit, which is now in its third reissuance (MRP 3.0). Through MRP 3.0, the city is required to take actions that minimize pollution entering the stormwater system and the San Francisco Bay watershed. We will go through the process of investigating and identifying the source with the residents. If it’s anything but rain, we don’t want it going down the drain.” If the city does not comply with the requirements of the MPR 3.0, it could face large fines. If a citizen brings a complaint under federal law, it is $68,000 per day, with no cap. articles.text: Payam Music opens first East Bay piano school in Piedmont Payam Music Director Dennis Ni outside the school with teachers Kiara Kramer, Gail Gallagher, and Judah Arrington. Payam Music opened its first piano school in the Easy Bay this past March at 4390 Piedmont Avenue. The school was founded in 2015 by Payam Khastkhodaei with the intention of innovating the way piano is taught to make it easier and fun for beginners. As a kid, Khastkhodaei really enjoyed playing the piano, but hated his lessons, which caused him to quit. He missed the piano so much that he eventually began playing again, rediscovering his love for it. It was in college, where he studied developmental psychology in pediatrics, that he developed a groundbreaking teaching methodology. “He was learning about language acquisition, and he thought hold on a moment. When people learn a new language they always learn to speak it first. If music is a language, then why is it taught the opposite way? He started teaching piano using what is now what we call the Payam method, which uses letters and numbers,” explained Chief Marketing Officer Deborah Kelson. The methodology uses alphanumeric notation rather than traditional sheet music to teach students to speak piano in a language they already know. Starting with letters and numbers to build confidence from day one. This has helped students understand intervals and note relationships sooner than the traditional sheet music. With the school’s in-house curriculum, every student learns based on their abilities, interests, and progress. They teach tradiTeachers personalize each lesson using Payam Music’s proprietary curriculum instead of traditional song books. tional classical music and pop or K-pop songs to bring fun into learning. “We have all of these songs that kids recognize and love, and so they’re really inspired to play, but also, because of the alphanumeric notation I mentioned, they’re able to play a song that they recognize by the end of their first lesson,” said Kelson. This innovative methodology has helped 96% of Payam Music students achieve a diploma level within four years, compared to a 2% national average for students reaching diploma level (in 12 years). Payam Music students even participate in a national arts competition. Every year, about 300,000 students participate in the National PTA Reflections Competition. In 2025, 15 of the school’s students won their district, with the majority being new to the competition, and four out of five state winners and national qualifiers came from the school. “We’re building a movement that challenges the traditional model of music education. Our methodology creates an environment where learning feels like play, and success is a natural result of students falling in love with piano,” said Khastkhodaei. Piedmont is currently the school’s fastest-growing location, and the school credits this to the community. “We really look for strong communities where education and music are valued. We want to find places where people are really excited about high-quality after-school enrichment. Those are the communities where we tend to open,” said Kelson. The company currently has eight locations open, with expansion plans for 2026. Lessons begin at age four with no upper age limit. Readers can sign up for a free orientation and a private one-on-one lesson on the company’s website, https://www.payammusic.com/.

At Piedmont High School the language department Singing Competition has become one of the most anticipated student events of the year. The competition is a lively showcase where music, culture, and classroom creativity converge. This semester’s lineup delivered an especially dynamic mix of performances, with each class bringing its own personality, language focus, and artistic flair to the stage. The day started with a win for an energetic performance by Ms. Freeland’s Spanish 3 class as they kicked things off with a bold mashup of “Danza Kuduro” and “NUEVAYoL.” The group’s confidence set a high bar early in the competition. Following that, Senora Sahagon’s AP Spanish class in period 2 took a different approach, leaning into nostalgia with “Ahora Te Puedes Marchar / Noches de Verano.” Their performance balanced humor and vocal strength, weaving together storytelling and expressive acting. Ms. Guillen’s Spanish 2 class brought a modern pop vibe with “Mía” in period 3. Their polished delivery and strong group cohesion made for a smooth, engaging performance. While less theatrical than some others, their consistency and musicality earned them steady applause. One of the most talked-about acts came from the middle school, with Shannon Fierro’s Spanish 1 class who delivered a high-energy Bad Bunny mashup featuring “Tití,” “DTMF,” and “Nueva Yol.” Their enthusiasm was infectious, and despite being younger than most competitors, they commanded the stage with surprising confidence. The crowd especially responded to their playful choreography and bold song choices. The competition then shifted linguistically and stylistically with Ms. Xia’s Chinese 4 Honors class, who performed in period 5. The cultural contrast added richness to the event, reminding the audience of the diversity within the language program. Ms. Xia’s Chinese 2 students won period 6 with a medley that stood out for its emotional range, moving from lighthearted and playful to reflective and bittersweet. The transitions between songs were handled smoothly, and their expressive delivery resonated strongly with the audience. Closing the competition was Ms. Freeland’s Spanish 3 which dominated period 7, featuring an original song titled “Sueño Grande,” written by student Eli Hauser. The performance was a standout moment, not just for its originality, but for its sincerity. The lyrics, centered on ambition and identity, gave the piece a personal depth that set it apart from the covers and mashups. Overall, this year’s competition highlighted not only musical talent but also the creativity and cultural engagement fostered within Piedmont High’s language programs. From reggaeton mashups to original songwriting to Mandarin classics, each performance reflected the unique voice of its class. More than just a contest, the event served as a celebration of language learning brought to life through music. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter with the Piedmont Post. articles.text: If the past few weeks felt full of climate conversation, you’re not alone. Between Earth Day and San Francisco Climate Week, people across the Bay Area have been surrounded by big ideas, activism, innovation, and urgency. And then, just like that, the calendar turns. The question is: what happens next? For some families, this is familiar territory. For others, it can feel overwhelming. Environmental justice work is deeply important, but it’s hard to know where to begin. What many adults underestimate is how much kids are already thinking about it. Today’s young people are far more aware of environmental change than many of us were at their age. Climate isn’t an abstract future problem; it already takes up real mental space, sometimes showing up as worry or anxiety. This must also shift the way we talk about and activate our responsibility in a more complicated time for our planet. I have vivid memories of family hikes on Earth Day or trying out non-aerosol hair products, small choices that felt somehow connected to the planet’s health. But while I grew up hearing that “kids are the future,” it didn’t feel as immediate or personal. My teenagers talk far more passionately about environmental issues in our community—like the impact flooding has on the health of our watersheds or the safety of our public transit systems—than I did when I was growing up. For many young people in the Bay Area, these changes are already immediate and local. At the Exploratorium, we have a literal front-row seat to climate change. From Piers 15 and 17, visitors encounter sea level rise not as an abstraction, but as something you can see and measure. So it’s no surprise we use this as an opportunity to turn our experiences and concerns into curiosity about what is happening, why it’s happening, and what we can do. One of the most striking ways to see this is during King Tides. A few times a year, alignment between the sun and the earth during a new or full moon raises tides one or two feet higher than normal. Along the waterfront, water will spill onto sidewalks, roadways, and even into homes and businesses. As many young people know, today’s extreme King Tides are the high tides of tomorrow. Once you’ve seen it, the questions come naturally: What happens next? Who is affected? What can be done? These shared moments matter because they make something big feel tangible. Later this year, the Exploratorium will open a free public field station on our front plaza—an outdoor space with exhibits and art focused on climate change and sea level rise, designed to bring more of these conversations into the open. But you don’t need to wait for an event or exhibit to keep the conversation going. Start at home. Notice what’s around you. Older kids and teens might track household energy use or learn about the watershed in their community. For younger children, a simple activity like Melting Ice and Rising Seas can help make those big ideas visible. Climate change is real, and it can feel overwhelming. But it’s also a space for curiosity, creativity, and shared problem-solving. So don’t let Earth Day be the only day this comes up. Keep asking. Keep noticing. Keep learning together. Because the most important part of the conversation isn’t having it once— it’s continuing it. Try the Melting Ice and Rising Seas activity at home, and explore more hands-on science at exploratorium.edu/snacks Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont High School girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan officially steps down after eight years in charge. Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan announced he is stepping down from his role following eight years at the helm. Chan was an assistant coach on the team in 2018 and was promoted to the lead role the following year. He helped lead PHS to the Division 2 North Coast Section title in 2019, and won Western Alameda County Conference titles in 2019 and 2024. He led the team to an NCS Finals appearance in 2025. Before Piedmont High, Chan coached at Skyline Lacrosse Club, which has been a feeder program for both the boys’ and girls’ sides. “I’ve been coaching for 20 years in total. When I coached U11 at Skyline the first season we went 0-11. The very last game, we finally scored a point. I thought, ‘Oh, this wasn’t a successful season,’ but then every girl came back. So, my measure of success then was just getting every girl to come back and play. That’s been my goal every single year; not necessarily to win or lose, but to make sure the girls had a great experience,” Chan said. Piedmont’s 2019 team was possibly its best team of all time. Elie Cole, Zoe Torok, Lily Keville, Widdy Tevis, and current assistant coach Sadie Tschider each went on to play at the collegiate level. His daughter Maria, eventually went on to play for the Coast Guard Academy. Tevis and Maria were juniors on that team, while Tschider was a sophomore and later became the school’s alltime leader in assists. “That same team was almost the same group of girls I coached in U11. We were good and had really strong players, and went up against great teams like Miramonte and Boo Dewitt, who was an All-American and plays at Florida. The focus of that group of girls was to get kids to play together. To get them to play as a team was in large part that they played so many years together. Their chemistry is really hard to recreate,” Chan said. “I told the girls at the end of the [2019] season that winning is really, really hard. For them to win, and win, and win and get that championship was from the fact they knew how to play together,” he added. The following two seasons in 2020 and 2021 were wiped out due to the global pandemic and you can’t help but wonder what those years would’ve looked like if COVID never happened. “In 2020 we had Ashley Nelson, who was the one that won our 2019 title despite being a defender. articles.text: Nate Welch, Ari Moskovitz place 4th in doubles Tennis star Lucas Smolko got the job done in his final Western Alameda County Conference tournament, winning the singles title for the third straight time on Saturday, May 2 at Chabot College in Hayward. He becomes the first male boys’ athlete to win three straight WACC titles and the second Piedmont High athlete to do so after Kaelli Thiel won the girls’ tournament in 2012, 2013, and 2015. Smolko faced Castro Valley’s Guhan Anandkumar in the final, winning in straight sets 6-2, 6-3. Smolko also faced Anankumar in last year’s semifinals, which featured strange mind games from the Trojans’ starter. Lucas was prepared for any antics, once again, and dispatched him handily. “It’s great to make history… Playing Guhan is tricky, I was thinking about it a lot going into today. I knew this match was inevitable and I’d end up playing Guhan in the final. I just knew to block out any mind games and if there are problems, not to be afraid to ask for line judges,” Smolko said. To get there, Smolko entered as the top seed, beating Alameda’s Johnny Sanchez 6-0, 6-1 in the first round. He followed up with a 6-0, 6-2 win over Castro Valley’s Matthew Rodriguez in the quarterfinals, and then defeated Bishop O’Dowd’s Marcello Sachelari 6-1, 6-3 in the semifinals. Also competing well in the tournament were the doubles team of senior Nate Welch and freshman Ari Moskovitz, taking fourth place in the doubles bracket. As the No. 3 seed, Welch and Moskovitz had a close fight in the first round with O’Dowd’s Nicolas Leduc and Matteo Mathlie-Zapien 7-6 (7-5), 6-4. They followed with a three-set win over O’Dowd’s Jack Gonzalez and James Hollins, 4-6, 7-6 (7-2), 10-8 in the quarterfinals. It was another three-set battle in the semifinals, where they lost to O’Dowd’s Lucas Tanaka and Oliver Liao, 6-1, 3-6, 6-3. Piedmont now prepares for the North Coast Section Individual Tournament on May 8-9, while the NCS Team Tournament begins May 12. Entering unseeded, the duo beat Berkeley’s Henri Andreini and Otter Carychao in three sets, 6-2, 4-6, 12-10. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, May 6, 2026 Sports Carlton Chan steps down as girls’ lacrosse coach Staff Photos Piedmont High School girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan officially steps down after eight years in charge. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse coach Carlton Chan announced he is stepping down from his role following eight years at the helm. Chan was an assistant coach on the team in 2018 and was promoted to the lead role the following year. He helped lead PHS to the Division 2 North Coast Section title in 2019, and won Western Alameda County Conference titles in 2019 and 2024. He led the team to an NCS Finals appearance in 2025. Before Piedmont High, Chan coached at Skyline Lacrosse Club, which has been a feeder program for both the boys’ and girls’ sides. “I’ve been coaching for 20 years in total. When I coached U11 at Skyline the first season we went 0-11. The very last game, we finally scored a point. I thought, ‘Oh, this wasn’t a successful season,’ but then every girl came back. So, my measure of success then was just getting every girl to come back and play. That’s been my goal every single year; not necessarily to win or lose, but to make sure the girls had a great experience,” Chan said. Piedmont’s 2019 team was possibly its best team of all time. Elie Cole, Zoe Torok, Lily Keville, Widdy Tevis, and current assistant coach Sadie Tschider each went on to play at the collegiate level. His daughter Maria, eventually went on to play for the Coast Guard Academy. Tevis and Maria were juniors on that team, while Tschider was a sophomore and later became the school’s alltime leader in assists. “That same team was almost the same group of girls I coached in U11. We were good and had really strong players, and went up against great teams like Miramonte and Boo Dewitt, who was an All-American and plays at Florida. The focus of that group of girls was to get kids to play together. To get them to play as a team was in large part that they played so many years together. Their chemistry is really hard to recreate,” Chan said. “I told the girls at the end of the [2019] season that winning is really, really hard. For them to win, and win, and win and get that championship was from the fact they knew how to play together,” he added. articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team had a historic day at Stafford Lake on Sunday, May 3, closing out a season that included two rainouts and only three completed races before the championship races coming up in two weeks. Racing in the East Bay/ Central League, Division 2, Piedmont High School earned 2nd place as a team for the day — the team’s first podium finish in memory — and finished 3rd overall for the season. The Stafford Lake course was demanding, with the high school race covering about 4 miles and 500 feet of climbing per lap, including steep climbs and technical descents. The Devo, junior development, course for middle school racers was shorter but still challenging, at about 2.4 miles and 400 feet of climbing. It was an emotional and long-awaited victory for Jasper, who has been working toward this goal for years. He was a series leader as a freshman, finished 2nd in JV1 as a sophomore, and finally reached his dream of winning a varsity race. With the win, Jasper secured the leader’s jersey for the 2026 Varsity season, as the fastest mountain biker in the East Bay/Central League. He will be competing in the Unbound Gravel, a 200-mile race in Emporia, Kansas at the end of the month. and plans to join the CalPoly SLO Cycling Team next year. The Piedmont girls also made history. In the season standings, Josephine finished 1st, Olivia 4th, and Mina 5th, a momentous milestone for Piedmont girls racing. Piedmont also saw breakthrough podium finishes from Zachary Carter, who placed 2nd in JV1 Boys D2, and Kai Hsu, who placed 5th in JV2 Boys D2. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team suffered a dramatic 8-7 loss to Berkeley at the Yellowjackets home field on Wednesday, April 29 to end their season, With an overall season record of 6 wins and 11 defeats, the Highlanders’ missed out on a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs. The loss came with some controversy, where Berkeley’s time keepers gave its team a huge favor at the end of the first quarter. The Highlanders committed a foul outside of the 12-meter circle with 12 seconds left on the clock. By rule, the clock should have continued rolling, but BHS stopped the clock, allowing their team to make a play in the process. Berkeley wound up scoring, which ultimately became the difference in the match. “It was a good game, but it came with some controversy. In the first quarter the clock should have run out. Instead, the Berkeley folks stopped the clock and that allowed Berkeley just enough time to make a run to the goal and score. That score mattered and Peyton Watson scored three goals in the final game of her Piedmont High career. articles.text: Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters. “New Japanese Clay” is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through June. The exhibition brings together modern and contemporary works that reimagine a centuries-old tradition in Japanese ceramics. Infused with vivid color and sculptural ambition, the pieces range from rugged, earthbound forms that evoke stone and soil to delicate constructions that appear as light as paper or billowing fabric. Museum officials said the exhibition reflects both Japan’s rich ceramic history and the increasingly global nature of contemporary art training and practice, as well as materials used. The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters who are expanding the expressive possibilities of clay. Robert Mintz, who organized the exhibition, said the featured artists build on the legacy of the mingei, or folk art, movement while forging distinctly experimental paths. “The artists in New Japanese Clay are challenging the conventions of functional ceramics and pivoting toward a purely sculptural experience,” Mintz said in a statement. “Their creations are meant to intrigue and delight; the vessel form is just a point of departure for spectacular experimentation.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/new-japanese-clay/.
articles.title: “New Japanese Clay” exhibit on view through June at Asian Art Museum exhibition

articles.text: Visit the Treasure Island Museum’s free public gallery to view its growing permanent collection and learn more about the island’s three defining eras: the 1939–40 Golden Gate International Exposition, the island’s decades as a U.S. Naval station, and its ongoing redevelopment. The museum is operated by a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage. The 1939 Exposition was held on Treasure Island in celebration of the city’s two newly-built bridges. The U.S Navy then acquired the land to use as a Naval Station from 1941 to 1997. The permanent collection includes artifacts from the exposition, such as decorative objects and cultural items, as well as photographs, postcards and ephemera that chronicle civilian and military life on the island. Artifacts range from exhibition objects like decorative Chinese dragons and a 16th-century Siamese ceramic bowl to mid-century memorabilia such as a baby contest trophy from the world’s fair. The collection also includes extensive photographs, postcards and ephemera documenting daily life on the island across generations. A mural on the museum’s back wall was designed by photo-realist Lowell Nesbitt, measuring 251 feet long and 26 feet high. The piece was commissioned for the opening of the museum, and represents scenes in the history of the Navy and Marine Corps in the Pacific since 1813. Treasure Island Museum has also developed an online collection that provides public access to digitized materials. Among the highlights is The Masthead, the naval base’s weekly newspaper, with issues from the World War II era available for viewing. Treasure Island Museum is open to the public Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and 12 p.m. to 7 p.m. on weekends. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/visit to learn more about the museum’s in-person and online offerings, and to view upcoming events and speaker series engagements. The museum is open seven days a week. Photo courtesy of SF.gov
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum offers glimpse into island’s rich past

articles.text: Showing at Toni Rembe Theater now through May 24 Photo courtesy of American Conservatory Theater The play features Kemi-Bo Jacobs as Agnes and Rory Alexander as William. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco closes out its 2025-26 season with the US premiere of Hamnet, showing onstage now through May 24. Adapted by Lolita Chakrabarti, who adapted the critically-acclaimed book Life of Pi, and directed by Erica Whyman, the play explores what happens when the plague steals 11-year-old Hamnet from his loving parents, Agnes and William Shakespeare, and they must each confront their loss alone. The death of Shakespeare’s son Hamnet has been thought to have influenced his writing, specifically his great tragedy Hamlet. Hamnet made its world premiere in April 2023 at the Swan Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon, and has its West Coast premiere on the A.C.T. stage. The play features Kemi-Bo Jacobs as Agnes and Rory Alexander as William. The creative team includes set and costume designer Tom Piper, lighting designer Prema Mehta, sound designer Simon Baker, music composer Oğuz Kaplangi, and movement director Ayşe Tashkiran. “I am delighted to be revisiting this extraordinary story for U.S. audiences, and to be making this production with a stellar line-up of performers,” Director Whyman said in a press release. “Kemi-Bo Jacobs and Rory Alexander are bringing Agnes and William alive on the stage with a luminous intelligence and a profound and shocking understanding of the love and loss that shaped their lives.” Visit https://www.act-sf. org/whats-on/2025-26-season/ hamnet/performances for showtimes and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: A.C.T. closes out 2025-26 season with Hamnet

articles.text: This summer the Bay Area will resonate with extraordinary music as the Golden Gate International Choral Festival welcomes over 450 choristers, adjudicators, and chaperones from around the globe for a week of breathtaking performances, cultural exchange, and artistic excellence. The festival takes place July 13-18, and is organized and hosted by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. The Festival stands as one of the world’s most celebrated gatherings of young singers. Under the visionary leadership of Artistic Director Eric Tuan, internationally recognized as one of the world’s premier youth choir conductors, the Festival promises performances of rare beauty, cultural significance, and emotional power. “The Golden Gate Festival is a place where young people from around the world build bridges between cultures,” says Tuan. “Even in a deeply divided world, the Festival offers us the chance to connect through the universal language of music, bringing our unique cultures and voices together to create international harmony. Children who sing together cannot build walls or create conflicts. They know in a deep, visceral way that what unites us is far greater than what divides us.” The Festival proudly welcomes eleven exceptional youth and children’s choirs from across the globe, including Guest Choir Young Voices of the Philippines (Philippines), as well as Cantabella Children’s Chorus (USA), E. Mikeladze Central Music School (Georgia), Ellerhein Girls’ Choir (Estonia), Girls Choir Canzona (Poland), Kajetán (Czechia), Singakademie Graz and Green Guys (Austria), Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió (Catalonia), and Vox Aurea (Finland). Guiding the festival is a distinguished panel of world-renowned adjudicators—María Guinand, Dr Maria Theresa Vizconde-Roldan, Jude B. Roldan, and Valérie Sainte-Agathe. The adult tickets range in price, while kids under 5 are free. The weeklong festival also includes Spotlight Concerts, free to the public. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival schedule can be found on their website, along with information on which concerts are free to the public or require paid admission. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ ggf-concerts-2026. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Big Hero 6 Disney’s animated Oscar nominated Big Hero 6 will appeal to an audience of kids and family. The narrative, a derivative of Marvel’s superhero characters, features 14-year-old Hiro Hamada (Ryan Potter), a nerdy, robotics obsessed kid. He lives in the futuristic Asian-like city of San Francisco where he hangs out with a cohort of extraordinary friends: GoGo Tanago (Jamie Chung), Wasabi (Damon Wayans, Jr.), and Honey Lemon (Genesis Rodriguez). Hiro spends his days submerged in techie stuff. At night, however, he engages in illegal robotic fight games. His older brother, Tadashi (Daniel Henney), worries about Hiro’s nighttime antics, so with the encouragement of both Hiro’s aunt, Cass (Maya Rudolph), and Tadashi, he agrees to visit the cutting-edge Institute of San Fransokyo. They hope to influence the young prodigy to give up his underground exploits, and come to the realization that there is a world beyond his own niche of homegrown high tech stuff. As it turns out, the visit to the university proves a success. Hiro, captivated, meets kindred spirits, sees advanced labs, and meets the distinguished Professor Callaghan (James Cromwell), head of robotics, and the inventor of a medical bot, Baymax (Scott Adsit), programed to care for his charge. It eventually becomes Hiro’s sidekick of sorts. Of course, there is a sudden turn of events, which impacts Hiro and his buds, and they soon discover that as a result, their lives have been turned upside down. What occurs? Well, they unexpectedly discover an ominous, dangerous plot that pulls the gang into a harrowing adventure that is brimming with fun, action, and imaginative science (an example being a swarm of buzzing microbots). Older kids, tweens and teens will find Big Hero 6 a compelling watch, and Hiro an interesting role model. The world of high tech/A.I. is upon us. Hiro is already there. Big Hero 6. Recall Snow White and the spiked apple; Cinderella, forced to scrub and clean; or Rapunzel, locked away in a high tower. The Oscar-winning animated feature Brave does star a strongwilled teenage princess, Merida (Kelly MacDonald), who rebels not against an unkind stepmother, but against her imperious mother, queen Elinor (Emma Thompson). The period is medieval Scotland, filled with crags and castles and rolling highlands. And there is, of course, Merida, with her massive ginger-colored tresses, a young royal who happens to identify with her father, onelegged, big lug King Fergus (Bill Connoly). She can ride like the wind, and is an expert archer (not unlike Katniss Everdeen of The Hunger Games), and would rather be racing horseback through the surrounding forests than spending time with the staid ladies of the court. Elinor, of course, has her own ideas of how a young princess should behave. But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender equality. In 1913, he gathered several successful Piedmont businessmen to purchase land opposite Piedmont Park, and hired Albert Farr to design the Piedmont Commercial Center, the first stores in Piedmont. articles.text: A seven-year-old watches her dog’s body language. Many new dog owners express concerns about the role children will play in a new dog’s life. It’s a true asset to have a dog who is comfortable with kids so you can feel confident the dog is reliable around them in public situations. But how do you help both your child and your new dog build a safe, respectful relationship? Here are a few tips! When you first bring home a dog, your child will likely be very excited and want to spend as much time as possible with their new companion. As the adult, it is your job to provide adequate supervision during these interactions. Young children (elementary school age and below) should never be left alone with a dog— no matter how friendly. Unfortunately, most bites occur in familiar settings due to lack of adult supervision. This also means simply being in the same room is not enough; your child and dog need your active attention. Be sure to educate your child on dog body language and canine social behavior. Kids need to understand stress signals such as a stiff body, lip licking, yawning, or turning away. Teach them to give the dog space when it walks away or hides. Most bites happen because a dog is fearful, not aggressive. Children must also learn that human signs of affection are not always interpreted

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Piedmont Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month and offers a great movie in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion to follow. The Flix Fest May selection is Ramen Girl, a 2009 romantic comedy-drama directed by Robert Allan Ackerman and starring Brittany Murphy as Abby, with Toshiyuki Nishida as Maezumi, whose powerful interactions as student and teacher provide cross-cultural lessons in understanding and communication. Abby finds herself abandoned by her boyfriend in Tokyo after impulsively traveling from the States to meet him, with no knowledge of Japanese and few personal contacts. The reality of her situation causes an emotional breakdown, which places her in a neighborhood ramen shop, where the owners offer a bowl of ramen as comfort for her obvious distress. During return visits to this shop, Abby sees the happiness that ramen brings to other customers and commits to becoming a ramen chef with the shop’s owner as her teacher, or sensei. Brittany Murphy brings her comedic skills to her role as Abby, despite the frustration she experiences from communicating with her incurably grumpy teacher, who speaks no English. The movie’s plot takes us through this often painful learning process culminating in the best scene of the film, when Maezumi confronts Abby with her inability to bring soul to her broth. Frustrated by his inability to communicate this core value for making ramen to Abby, Maezumi visits his mother with Abby to get his mother’s advice. She tells Abby to put her tears in the broth to create a unique flavor for her ramen. This elicits the appropriate reaction from neighbors who are tasting her ramen for the first time. Realizing that Maezumi has found his successor, he retires after 40 years as a Master Chef, leaving Abby to sustain his legacy! Ramen Girl will be screened on Thursday, May 14, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone over 18. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The next movie will be Before Sunrise, a 1995 romance film, which will be shown on June 11 at 4 p.m., rather than the normal time. Kids and Dogs: Building safe relationships A seven-year-old watches her dog’s body language. By Sierra Berrick Many new dog owners express concerns about the role children will play in a new dog’s life. It’s a true asset to have a dog who is comfortable with kids so you can feel confident the dog is reliable around them in public situations. But how do you help both your child and your new dog build a safe, respectful relationship? Here are a few tips! When you first bring home a dog, your child will likely be very excited and want to spend as much time as possible with their new companion. As the adult, it is your job to provide adequate supervision during these interactions. Young children (elementary school age and below) should never be left alone with a dog— no matter how friendly. Unfortunately, most bites occur in familiar settings due to lack of adult supervision. This also means simply being in the same room is not enough; your child and dog need your active attention. Be sure to educate your child on dog body language and canine social behavior. Kids need to understand stress signals such as a stiff body, lip licking, yawning, or turning away. Teach them to give the dog space when it walks away or hides. Most bites happen because a dog is fearful, not aggressive. Children must also learn that human signs of affection are not always interpreted the same way by dogs. This means no climbing, hugging, or pulling. Encourage your child to let the dog come to them first— and to respect the dog’s choice if they decline. It is equally important to teach both your dog and your child safe ways to interact. Encourage kids to use calm voices and to “be a tree” (stand still) if a dog becomes overly excited. Remind them to use “gentle hands” and avoid faceto-face contact. Train your dog to follow basic cues like sit, stay, leave it, and off to help them remain calm around children. Reward calm behavior and maintain clear boundaries around unsafe actions like mouthing, even if it seems gentle. You can also gradually desensitize your dog to noise and sudden movement, since children tend to be active and unpredictable. Remember, as the adult, it is your responsibility to set clear rules and boundaries. Modeling positive interactions is one of the most effective ways to teach your child how to behave around their new furry friend. Providing your dog with a safe, kid-free space when they feel overwhelmed will also help them feel secure in the home. The walkers climbed up and across King, and as they approached Hampton, they spotted a Piedmont Police car parked next to Crocker/Bear Park. Officer Hugo Diaz was nearby chatting with a resident. The walkers soon surrounded him, and the group moved into the park for some shade — but not before snapping a group photo with Officer Diaz and the Benny Bufano ground-granite Nursing Bear and Cubs sculpture. The piece, more than 5 feet tall and 2.5 tons, has stood in the park since 1980. It is No. 9 in a limited edition of 25, with only five believed to be in the Bay Area. Officer Diaz told the walkers he is an Oakland native. He was an art major at Cal State East Bay and did graduate work in art but ultimately decided there were greater career opportunities in police work. He joined PPD eight years ago, and his background made him a natural fit as the department's Juvenile Liaison Officer with Piedmont's schools. The walkers brought plenty of questions. Bad driving topped the list. One walker, who lives on Oakland Avenue, said he once watched a car barrel down his busy street at 58 mph. Drivers running stop signs also leave walkers uneasy. And students on electric bikes are often seen riding at high, unsafe speeds. Middle-school boys, in particular, seem to be a problem. Officer Diaz said he has been in regular communications with the schools about it, but parents need to be aware of the problem and the danger to their kids. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors took a recent excursion, venturing off its usual path, to get two personal group tours, including a one-hour tour of Heath Ceramics in Sausalito. Each and every piece of the dinnerware Heath produces – start-to-finish – from being formed, glazed, trimmed and fired, is made here by a team of 40 craftspeople, almost exactly as it has been since the beginning. The tour took the group through the building’s light-filled courtyard, showroom, and sweeping semi-circle factory. Heath’s dinnerware offers strong color statements, with the intensity softened by the earthy influence of the manganese clay body. Its classic glazes are built around the natural variation and depth present in raw glaze ingredients like iron, copper, cobalt, and manganese. Their earthy quality pairs well with other natural materials like wood and stone. In its showroom, Heath even offers discounted dinnerware and one-of-a-kind prototypes that don’t quite meet its first quality standards. Heath Ceramics began as a small-scale pottery business in 1948, with Edith and Brian Heath, and has evolved into a pure and simple way of life and business that shares many forms of expression through the dinnerware it creates. Their pottery is now used by the renowned Chez Panisse of Berkeley! After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors had built up an appetite, so ventured to nearby Joinery Beer Hall + Rotisserie on the Sausalito waterfront for a laidback lunch. Here, the Seniors enjoyed hearty, seasonal fare in a warm, communal setting. Their hearty fried chicken sandwich was a fan favorite! After lunch, the Seniors went to take their second guided tour of the day, this time at the Bay Model, again in Sausalito. This is a one-of-its-kind model in the entire world! The model is a working hydraulic scale model of the San Francisco Bay and Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta System. While the Bay Model is still operational, it is no longer used for scientific research but is instead open to the public alongside educational exhibits about Bay hydrology. It provides visitors a unique opportunity to view the complete bay-delta system at a glance. She is a bit older but eats a lot healthier. I have heart disease in my family but she has Alzheimer’s in hers. No one knows who will be called upon to do the hard work of the vows. As I watched the couples at Mayo one in the wheelchair and one pushing, it was touching to see that in a world filled with divorce, betrayal and broken promises some people really do keep their wedding vows. The love and care I witnessed — an understanding smile, an arm around the shoulder, two gnarled hands entwined brought me to tears. I began to realize I was at a holy place. I usually take lots of photos when I travel, I am obsessed with documenting my experiences but not here. It seemed too sacred a place to profane with a photo. I was like Moses at the burning bush, needing to take off my shoes because I was standing on holy ground. You must apply to the Mayo Clinic and hope you are accepted. They want to think they can help you before you schlep to the clinic. It seems that they like challenges, people that have seen other doctors but still don’t have a diagnosis. That was me, despite having excellent doctors who are part of the Stanford medical group after five years they have still not been able to figure out for sure why I am increasingly unable to walk or stand for long. My local doctors endorsed the idea of trying to get another opinion from Mayo. So, I sent off my application and was told that the Mayo Clinic closest to me in Scottsdale, Arizona was booked up but they could see me at the mother location in Rochester, Minnesota. After years of listening to Garrison Keillor talk about Minnesota on the Prairie Home Companion radio show I was excited to visit the land of 10,000 lakes. Rochester is a town of 120,000 about an hour’s drive southwest of Minneapolis. How this gleaming chrome and glass 19 story skyscraper came to rise out of this agricultural landscape is amazing. You can see it from the distance the way a traveler in France can see from a great distance Chartres cathedral rising out of the cornfields. I was here to see neurologist Dr. Brian Keegan a short, fit, balding Canadian who had traded in the white doctor’s coat for a tight blue sport jacket. He exuded both efficiency and compassion. When he spoke not a word was wasted — he got right to the point he had a lot of sick people to see, and he was not going to dawdle. And yet when you talked to him it seemed as though you had all the time in the world to share your story. It was evident his listening stills were highly tuned. I immediately felt I was in good hands. He set me up with an appointment in the physical therapy department and I was assigned to Heather Ducharme. It is hard to explain, but talking with her was being enveloped in a warm hug. Her face exuded compassion and amazing empathy. I wanted to bottle her expression and take it home with me. She brainstormed with me some ways we could deal with my increasingly feeble legs and improve my walking ability. I left with a list of home exercises for balance and strength. I also met with Dr. Jennifer Dens Higano in the physical medicine department. She was unhurried and focused and had a lovely calming sense about her. She explained the different types of neuropathies and helped me understand more about my malady. I asked her where she was from because she did not have that Minnesota accent (think movie Fargo). “I’m from northern Minnesota where we have a lot more lakes. I don’t know what the Mayo Brothers were thinking choosing to settle in the only county in MN that doesn’t have a lake!” I wish all doctors were so winsome and down to earth. I was not able to get an appointment with any of the 20 doctors in the rheumatology dept. during the week I was in MN, so I was advised to register myself as a “checker.” You register with the front desk and park yourself in the huge waiting room and wait for someone to cancel or not show up for their appointment.
